h: Five centuries of the Navy in one walk
p: Here's why people bang on about this place. Within a short stroll you can stand on the deck of HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship at the Battle of Trafalgar in 1805, then walk a few minutes and come face to face with what's left of the Mary Rose, Henry VIII's warship that sank in 1545 and was raised from the Solent in 1982. That's hundreds of years of British naval history, side by side, and it's genuinely jaw-dropping in person.

Then there's HMS Warrior. When she was launched in 1860 she was the Navy's first iron-hulled, armoured warship, and walking her long gun decks gives you a real sense of how quickly ships were changing in the Victorian age. Little HMS M.33 is a survivor from the First World War and the Gallipoli campaign, and she's a fascinating contrast to the giants around her.

The Mary Rose Museum is the one not to rush. Alongside the hull itself are thousands of objects recovered with her, from weapons to everyday bits and bobs, and the personal items are what really stick with people. Older kids who think they're not bothered about history are often the ones asking the most questions by the end.

Plan your must-sees and get to them first, while legs are fresh. Allow a full day if you want to do the big three properly, and wear comfy shoes, because there's a lot of standing, climbing and ducking under low beams on the ships. Ladders and steep steps are part of the experience on board, so let anyone with mobility worries know before you go.

Some of the attractions on the wider ticket are across the harbour in Gosport, reached by water, so check how they link up if you fancy squeezing those in. Many families find spreading the visit across two days far more enjoyable than trying to cram it into one.

Next door, Gunwharf Quays has places to eat and the Spinnaker Tower, and Old Portsmouth's cobbled streets and the Round Tower are a lovely stroll at the end of the day, with the harbour mouth right in front of you.
